items.title: Oil pullback eases pressure on bonds and stocks
items.excerpt: Hopes of a diplomatic opening in the Iran war pulled oil down and stocks up, and took some of the volatility out of Treasuries. Brent settled around $104 after the New York Times reported that Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart nuclear talks. The S&P 500 rose 0.5%, and a chipmaker gauge had its longest weekly advance since May. Thirty-year yields stayed at a two-decade high and edged only slightly higher. Money markets still price three Federal Reserve hikes over the next year, because high energy costs are still feeding inflation.

spx.mechanism: Chipmakers extended their longest weekly advance since May, and those companies make up a large part of the US indices. Brent’s fall toward $104 after Iran’s Hormuz proposal also eased inflation worries.
spx.outlook: Upward bias if oil keeps easing. With money markets pricing three Fed hikes and the 30-year yield near a two-decade high, rising yields are the main risk.

ndx.mechanism: Chipmakers extended their longest weekly advance since May, and those companies make up a large part of the US indices. Brent’s fall toward $104 after Iran’s Hormuz proposal also eased inflation worries.
ndx.outlook: Upward bias if oil keeps easing. With money markets pricing three Fed hikes and the 30-year yield near a two-decade high, rising yields are the main risk.

dji.mechanism: Brent’s fall toward $104 after Iran offered to reopen Hormuz eased the inflation worry that had pushed up rate-hike bets, so investors paid more for US shares. Calmer Treasuries also removed some of the week’s pressure on stock valuations.
dji.outlook: Upward bias if oil keeps easing. With money markets pricing three Fed hikes and the 30-year yield near a two-decade high, rising yields are the main risk.

items.title: Higher oil prices revive inflation and bond-market worries
items.excerpt: Bond volatility made traders reluctant to take risk. Stocks wavered on the worry that high oil prices will add to inflation and push the Federal Reserve to raise rates. Thirty-year yields hit the highest level since 2004, and a larger Treasury buyback did not calm the sell-off. Brent settled near $107 after reports that the US and Iran are exploring a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz. Money markets fully price three Fed hikes over the next year. Investors are also asking for more yield because of government spending and corporate borrowing for the AI build-out.

items.title: Inflation concerns push up yields and weigh on equities
items.excerpt: Stocks fell with bonds as higher oil revived inflation worries, reinforced by US business activity rising at the fastest pace since 2021. Brent settled around $103. A weak $70 billion sale of five-year notes pushed Treasury yields on most maturities to almost two-decade highs, and the dollar rose against the major currencies. Both manufacturing and services reported stronger orders and output. Fed Governor Michael Barr said further tightening is likely needed to get inflation back to target. Money markets fully price three hikes over the next year.

items.title: Japan: chip demand and dividend buying lift the Nikkei
items.excerpt: The Nikkei rose for a fifth straight session on Friday, up 1.30% to 66,364.20, and just over 2% for the holiday-shortened week. Topix rose 1.31% to 4,128.59. Daiwa strategist Daisuke Hashizume said investors bought before Monday’s deadline to qualify for interim dividends, but chip demand was the larger support. Bank shares, which tend to pay higher dividends, rose 4.08% and led the Tokyo Stock Exchange’s 33 industry groups: Mitsubishi UFJ gained 3.95% and Sumitomo Mitsui 3.59%. Tokyo Electron rose 4.82% and Advantest 2.84%, the biggest contributors to the Nikkei’s gain. Of the 225 names, 171 rose and 51 fell.

nky.mechanism: Tokyo Electron (+4.82%) and Advantest (+2.84%) were the largest contributors, so the chip rally pulled the Nikkei up with them. Bank shares rose 4.08% as investors bought before Monday’s interim-dividend deadline. That deadline is a one-session reason; the chip buying is the one that can last past Monday.
nky.outlook: The rise can continue if chip names such as Tokyo Electron and Advantest keep attracting buyers. It weakens if that chip bid fades after Monday’s dividend cutoff, or if a technology sell-off, like Friday’s 3.18% drop in SoftBank, spreads.

items.title: ECB research: earnings expectations underpin the AI equity rally
items.excerpt: ECB research highlights AI-linked profit expectations and the risk of an abrupt change in sentiment.

items.title: ECB bulletin reviews inflation risks and September tightening
items.excerpt: The bulletin reiterates the September 10 rate increase and inflation risks; publication this week does not make that an additional hike.

items.title: ECB research explains how US rate expectations spill into Europe
items.excerpt: US policy expectations can affect European financial conditions even when the ECB itself does not change rates.

items.title: SNB holds its policy rate at zero
items.excerpt: On 24 September the Swiss National Bank left its policy rate at 0%. Sight deposits at the SNB are paid that rate up to a threshold; above it, the discount stays at 0.25 percentage points. The SNB said it is still willing to buy or sell foreign currency if that is needed to keep monetary conditions appropriate. Inflation rose from 0.6% in May to 0.8% in August, mainly because oil-product prices pushed goods inflation positive for the first time since May 2024. The Bank said medium-term inflation pressure has increased only slightly, and that energy inflation, now elevated, is likely to ease over 2027.

items.title: RBA board member examines wage-price spiral risk
items.excerpt: On 22 September, RBA board member Iain Ross spoke in a personal capacity, not for the nine-member Monetary Policy Board. His argument is that Australia’s labour-market rules today are different from the 1970s and 1980s, when wages and prices chased each other. He said there is no evidence of a wage-price spiral now, and that recent data make one unlikely. A spiral, as he defined it, would start with a demand or cost shock, firms raising prices, and workers then winning wage rises that push costs and prices up again.

items.title: Collins explains why she supported the Fed rate increase
items.excerpt: Fed official Collins cited persistent inflation and energy risks in explaining her support for tighter policy.

items.title: Japan’s finance minister flags US concern over yen weakness
items.excerpt: Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Friday that President Trump, at Tuesday’s New York meeting with Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, raised the weak yen. Takaichi confirmed it: the US side said the weak yen was making trade difficult, and she replied that an undervalued yen is a problem in principle. She said the meeting did not discuss monetary or fiscal policy, and that her government’s economic stance is unchanged. Katayama presented this as a shared Tokyo–Washington worry about the yen’s slide, even after their joint intervention in July. It is a currency comment, not a new Bank of Japan rate decision.

jpy.mechanism: The risk of official yen buying makes bets against the yen less attractive. Buying back yen supports it, which means USD/JPY falls.
jpy.outlook: USD/JPY could fall further if intervention warnings intensify. Stronger US rate expectations work in the opposite direction; confidence is limited.

items.title: China leaves one-year and five-year loan prime rates unchanged
items.excerpt: China left the one-year loan prime rate at 3.00% and the five-year rate at 3.50% on Sunday, the 16th month without a change. All 21 respondents in a Reuters survey had expected no move. Mizuho’s Serena Zhou said that unless domestic demand weakens much more, broad easing in the fourth quarter is less likely while the Federal Reserve is more hawkish. BNP Paribas’s Jacqueline Rong said China is late in its rate-cutting cycle and her base case is that the People’s Bank stays on hold for the rest of the year. The loan prime rate is a bank lending benchmark, not the Fed’s policy rate.

items.title: US says details of China trade talks will follow on Monday
items.excerpt: Greer said further trade-deal details were due Monday. Until terms are released, the effect on demand and tariffs remains uncertain.

items.title: Natural gas retreats after a sharp supply-driven rally
items.excerpt: On Friday, US natural gas fell to $3.15 per MMBtu as traders took profits after Thursday’s jump to a 13-week high. TC Energy’s Columbia Gas Transmission pipeline in Appalachia declared force majeure after an unexpected mechanical fault in West Virginia; that outage had produced the largest one-day price gain since January. EIA inventories rose 53 Bcf in the week ended 18 September, cutting the surplus over the five-year average to 95 Bcf from 118 Bcf, after hot weather lifted cooling demand. Flows to the nine major LNG plants averaged 17.8 bcfd in September, up from 17.2 bcfd in August, even with the 0.8-bcfd Cove Point plant offline for maintenance. September production is still near a record 112.8 bcfd, but daily output has been falling in Louisiana and West Virginia.

ng.mechanism: Thursday’s force majeure on TC Energy’s Columbia Gas line in West Virginia tightened Appalachian supply and drove the largest one-day gain since January. Friday’s fall to $3.15 was traders selling to bank that gain. The outage, the smaller 53 Bcf storage build, and falling daily output in Louisiana and West Virginia are still the supply backdrop.
ng.outlook: The Friday drop can extend if the Columbia Gas fault is fixed and traders keep taking profits. Prices can turn back up if the force majeure stays in place, daily output in Louisiana and West Virginia keeps falling, or LNG feedgas stays near 17.8 bcfd. The next EIA storage print is the check.

items.title: Gas storage build is below the seasonal average
items.excerpt: On Thursday, US natural gas rose to $3.2 per MMBtu, the highest since 8 July. Energy firms added 53 billion cubic feet in the week ended 18 September, below the 77 bcf added a year earlier and the five-year average of 76 bcf, as hot weather boosted cooling demand. Inventories stood 2.9% above normal, down from 3.7% the week before. Lower-48 production was on track to fall to an 11-week low of 108.4 bcfd on Thursday, mainly in Louisiana and West Virginia. Average flows to the nine major LNG plants reached 17.8 bcfd in September, up from 17.2 bcfd in August, despite the planned shutdown of Berkshire Hathaway’s 0.8-bcfd Cove Point plant.

ng.mechanism: A 53 bcf storage build, against a five-year average of 76 bcf, leaves a thinner cushion after a hot week of cooling demand. Output heading for an 11-week low of 108.4 bcfd, led by Louisiana and West Virginia, means less gas coming to market on the day. That can lift the price; it does not stop a later round of profit-taking.
ng.outlook: The Thursday rise holds if the storage surplus keeps shrinking and Louisiana and West Virginia output stays weak. It fades if production recovers, weather turns milder through early October, or Cove Point’s 0.8 bcfd maintenance ends and changes the LNG balance. The next EIA release is the check.

items.excerpt: Official weekly inventory report. This rolling source updates each Thursday; use its displayed release date when cross-checking.

items.title: Wheat: export demand, planting and Black Sea risks
items.excerpt: Jack Scoville’s 25 September note said wheat was lower in both US markets while the US–China summit and the Ukraine–Russia war continued. Both sides of that war report an export pace more than 50% below a year ago. US weekly export sales were average, not strong. Winter-wheat planting is 19% complete and the spring-wheat harvest is finished. Chicago’s trend is mixed to down: December support at 685, 677 and 665 cents, resistance at 730, 736 and 742.

wh.mechanism: US weekly export sales were only average, so there was no demand surprise to bid wheat up. At the same time Ukraine and Russia each report exports more than 50% below last year, which keeps a supply risk under the market. Those two facts pull in opposite directions, which matches Scoville’s mixed-to-down Chicago trend.
wh.outlook: Prices can keep easing if export sales stay average and planting reaches beyond the current 19% of winter wheat without a weather problem. They can turn up if Black Sea shipments fall further from the already-halved pace, or if the next weekly sales report is clearly stronger. December Chicago support on this note is 685 cents.

items.title: Grain market commentary on export demand and trade talks
items.excerpt: Broker research provides agricultural context; commentary is an analyst view rather than an official data release.

items.title: A bond manager sees value after the Treasury sell-off
items.excerpt: Bloomberg reported that Lombard Odier Investment Management has turned overweight US Treasuries for the first time in at least five years. The firm’s stated reason is that the higher yields now look more attractive than stocks. The rest of the piece was not available beyond that lead, so this is the manager’s positioning, not a full account of why yields moved.

items.title: Gold rebounds intraday but faces weekly rate pressure
items.excerpt: Friday’s oil pullback helped gold, while higher yields weighed on its weekly performance. Silver is related precious-metal context, not the identical instrument.

au.mechanism: Lower oil prices can reduce inflation and rate-hike concerns. Lower expected interest returns on cash reduce the opportunity cost of owning gold, which pays no interest.
au.outlook: Gold has rebound potential if yields ease. A renewed oil shock and stronger rate-hike expectations could reverse that support.

items.title: Federal Reserve September policy decision
items.excerpt: The Fed raised its target range to 3.75–4.00%. This predates the current news week.

items.title: Bank of England September policy decision
items.excerpt: Bank Rate stayed at 3.75%; three of nine members preferred a rise to 4%. This is an earlier decision.

items.title: Hong Kong shares fall in holiday-thinned trading
items.excerpt: The Hang Seng fell 1% on Friday to 24,510.09, a two-month low, in holiday-thinned trade. The Hang Seng China Enterprises Index fell 1.2%. Insurance and technology led the drop: AIA lost 2.7% and Alibaba 1.5%. Volumes were light ahead of the Mid-Autumn Festival. Mainland markets and southbound Stock Connect were closed and reopen on Monday. Investors were waiting on Thursday’s Trump–Xi summit in Washington. ANZ’s Khoon Goh said it produced no breakthrough on AI, trade, Taiwan or Iran, but did set a floor under the relationship. UBP’s Carlos Casanova said the trade truce was extended while technology and geopolitics remain unresolved; the next test is the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

hsi.mechanism: AIA (−2.7%) and Alibaba (−1.5%) are heavy index names, so their drops pull the Hang Seng down. Southbound Stock Connect was shut and mainland markets were closed, so the usual mainland bid was absent and the remaining trade was thin. Thin trade can make a 1% index move larger than the news alone would.
hsi.outlook: A rebound needs either a reopening of Stock Connect on Monday with mainland buying, or a concrete result from the Trump–Xi talks. Goh’s point was that the summit only set a floor, and Casanova still sees technology and geopolitics unresolved, so reopening the connect by itself is not a reason to expect the 24,510 low to reverse.

items.excerpt: A consultation response on MiCAR: regulatory background, not an enacted rule or proof of a particular token’s price driver.

items.scope: Earlier policy decision · not a new daily catalyst
items.excerpt: On 18 September, the BOJ raised its overnight rate target to around 1.25%. This is an earlier policy baseline, not evidence of a new rate increase this week.

items.title: Stocks jump on AI optimism as AMD tops $1 trillion
items.excerpt: A rally in technology giants sent stocks to their best day since early August: the Nasdaq 100 rose 2.8% and the S&P 500 1.5%. Chipmakers surged as early signs of success for Meta’s AI agent sparked enthusiasm; Meta jumped 11% and AMD topped $1 trillion in market value. Oil sank on hopes for diplomatic efforts to end the war in Iran, Brent settled around $100 and Treasury 10-year yields fell below 5%.

ndx.mechanism: The Nasdaq is weighted toward large technology and chip companies, so an 11% jump in Meta and AMD’s move past $1 trillion lift the index directly. Cheaper oil and a 10-year yield back below 5% also make those companies’ future profits worth more today.
ndx.outlook: Upward bias while the AI rally broadens and the 10-year stays under 5%. It fades if oil rebounds or the Fed signals more hikes.

us10y.mechanism: Brent’s drop to about $100 eased fears that oil would keep inflation high, so investors accepted a lower yield and bought Treasuries. A yield below 5% means bond prices rose.
us10y.outlook: The yield stays lower only if oil keeps falling. A rebound in crude or hawkish Fed speakers would push it back above 5%.

items.title: Brent falls to $100 as Strait of Hormuz oil flows increase
items.excerpt: The October WTI contract, which expires Tuesday, fell about 4.5% and Brent settled 3.4% lower near $100 for a fourth straight loss. Saudi oil moving through Hormuz averaged about 2.9 million barrels a day in the six days to 18 September, up from about 700,000 in August (JPMorgan satellite data), and Trump told Fox News he would “probably” be open to meeting Iran’s President Pezeshkian at the UN General Assembly.

wti.mechanism: More Saudi barrels getting through Hormuz and the prospect of US–Iran talks reduce the risk of a supply shortage. Traders then pay less of a premium for crude, so WTI falls.
wti.outlook: Downward bias while Hormuz flows keep rising. The drop reverses if the UN talks fail or drone attacks hit Saudi exports again.

items.title: Nasdaq notches another new high
items.excerpt: The Nasdaq Composite rose 0.5% to 27,244, a new record close, as several AI stocks kept climbing, while the Dow fell 0.4% and the S&P 500 was fractionally lower. WTI crude fell for a fifth straight day after Saudi Arabia said it was close to reopening a key oil pipeline damaged in a drone attack.

ndx.mechanism: Continued buying in AI and chip shares lifts the Nasdaq more than the Dow or S&P, because those stocks make up a larger share of it. A fifth day of falling oil also eases inflation worries that would otherwise weigh on growth stocks.
ndx.outlook: Upward bias while AI buying continues. The risk is higher Treasury yields, which would cut the value of future tech earnings.

items.title: US stocks fall as 10-year Treasury yield hits highest since 2007
items.excerpt: US shares fell and the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield jumped 13.89 basis points to 5.106%, its highest since 2007 and biggest one-day rise since April 2025, after data showed US business activity racing to a more-than-five-year high in September. The Treasury drew very weak demand for a $70 billion five-year note sale, which sold at the highest auction yield since 2007. The Nasdaq Composite fell 1.13%, a sharp reversal after a record high on Tuesday; the S&P 500 dropped 0.75% and the Dow 0.68%.

ndx.mechanism: A 10-year yield above 5.1% lowers today’s value of profits expected far in the future, and Nasdaq technology companies depend most on those future profits. That is why the Nasdaq fell more than the S&P 500 or the Dow.
ndx.outlook: Downward pressure while yields stay above 5%. Next check: whether October Fed hike odds keep rising.

us10y.mechanism: Business activity at a more-than-five-year high raised the expected path of Fed rates, and very weak demand at the $70 billion five-year auction forced sellers to offer a higher yield. Higher yields mean Treasury prices fell.
us10y.outlook: Upward bias while the data stay strong and Fed hike odds rise. A softer inflation print or a better-received auction would ease it.

items.title: Oil settles up around 4% as Iran’s president vows to never surrender
items.excerpt: Brent settled up $3.83, or 3.86%, at $103.08 and November WTI gained $1.64, or 1.81%, to $92.16, as traders weighed Iranian President Pezeshkian’s vow never to surrender a day after Trump warned he could “annihilate” Iran. Early on Wednesday, WTI had touched its lowest since 1 September.

wti.mechanism: The printed −2.6% is a contract roll, not a price fall: Yahoo’s continuous WTI series switched from the expired October contract ($94.59 on Tuesday) to November, which closed at $92.16. On the same November contract, WTI actually rose 1.81% as Iran’s defiance revived the supply-risk premium.
wti.outlook: Upward risk while US–Iran rhetoric escalates. Compare like-for-like November prices, not the rolled series.

items.title: Japanese stocks mixed despite tech rally
items.excerpt: The Nikkei 225 closed at 65,513.99, up 495.04 points (0.76%), as it caught up with AI and semiconductor gains made during Japan’s Silver Week holiday (19–23 September), when the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index surged more than 8%. Tokyo Electron and Advantest rose about 2% and 3%, while rising government bond yields held back the broader market.

nky.mechanism: Chip-equipment makers such as Advantest and Tokyo Electron carry heavy weights in the price-weighted Nikkei, so their catch-up with the 8% US chip rally lifted the index. Rising government bond yields weighed on the rest of the market, which is why gains faded.
nky.outlook: Upward bias while US chip stocks hold their gains. Rising JGB yields are the main risk to the rally.

items.title: Dollar-yen recovers losses from rate check
items.excerpt: USD/JPY traded at 157.335 in New York, up 0.603 yen, recovering gains given up on 18 September after Japanese media reported a Bank of Japan “rate check”, a possible step before intervention. With Tokyo shut for the Silver Week holiday, traders judged that the fall had gone too far and that intervention at these levels was unlikely.

jpy.mechanism: The Fed’s hike and hawkish Fed speakers keep US rates well above Japan’s 1.25%, so holding dollars pays more than holding yen. Once the intervention scare faded, that rate gap pushed USD/JPY back up.
jpy.outlook: Upward bias while the US–Japan rate gap stays wide. Any real Japanese intervention would reverse it sharply.

items.title: Swiss franc gains as US dollar declines on increased risk appetite
items.excerpt: USD/CHF fell for a fourth consecutive day to about 0.8200 as the US dollar declined on risk-on sentiment around trade and diplomatic prospects, with traders watching the upcoming US–China summit. UOB strategists said upside momentum had faded and expected a 0.8155–0.8255 range.

chf.mechanism: Hopes for US–China and US–Iran diplomacy reduced demand for the dollar as a haven, so the dollar gave back part of the previous week’s gain against the franc. The Fed’s hawkish tone limited the fall.
chf.outlook: Range-bound between about 0.8155 and 0.8255. A break higher needs a wider US rate advantage.

items.title: British pound sells off as US surveys outpace the UK’s
items.excerpt: Wednesday’s flash PMIs showed US business growing at its fastest pace since July 2021, with services at 58.7 against a 56 forecast, while UK services slipped to a three-month low of 51.7. GBP/USD fell to its lowest since early July, and Fed Governor Barr said further increases are likely to be needed.

gbp.mechanism: Strong US data and Barr’s comments raised the chance of another Fed hike, while weaker UK activity makes a Bank of England hike less likely. Money follows the higher expected return, so the dollar gained against sterling.
gbp.outlook: Downward bias while the US–UK growth and rate gap widens. The Bank of England speakers on Thursday are the next check.

items.title: Australian dollar tumbles amid soaring US yields, ahead of jobs data
items.excerpt: AUD/USD slid more than 1% to 0.7039 from a peak of 0.7118 as the US 10-year yield surged 15.5 basis points to 5.11%, its highest since 2007, on strong US PMIs that reinforced the case for more Fed tightening. In Australia, September’s manufacturing PMI contracted and the composite PMI fell from 52.7 to 50.8.

aud.mechanism: A jump in US yields widens the return from holding dollars over Australian dollars, and the Aussie is also sold when global risk appetite falls. Weak Australian PMIs added to the pressure.
aud.outlook: Downward bias while US yields stay above 5%. An RBA hike on 29 September, which ING expects, would support the currency.

items.title: RBA preview: a decisive hike to keep inflation in check
items.excerpt: ING said the Australian dollar had a rough week, hit by poor risk sentiment and the global bond selloff, and that its fair-value model shows AUD/USD undervalued beyond 1.5 standard deviations. Markets price 22bp for the RBA on 29 September, while Fed funds futures price 90bp of US hikes by July 2027.

aud.mechanism: The week’s global bond selloff, led by US yields above 5%, made dollar assets pay more and hit risk-sensitive currencies like the Aussie. With markets pricing far more US than Australian tightening, the rate gap moved against AUD.
aud.outlook: ING expects a 25bp RBA hike on 29 September and sees the decline as overdone, with a year-end target of 0.72. A test below 0.700 is the near-term risk.

items.title: Nymex climbs amid near-term tightening
items.excerpt: October gas futures jumped 12.9¢ on Tuesday to $2.965 per million Btu. Gelber & Associates put US production plus Canadian imports at 115.6 bcf/d, “its weakest level in two weeks”, while residential and commercial demand rose 28% to 11.2 bcf/d as a brief cool shot reached key consuming regions and power burn rebounded 6% to 41.1 bcf/d.

ng.mechanism: Lower supply and higher heating and power demand on the same day tighten the near-term gas balance, so buyers pay more for the October contract. That recovered Monday’s fall.
ng.outlook: Gains are fragile: forecasts show the heating lift fading as temperatures moderate into early October. Thursday’s EIA storage report is the next check.

items.title: UK gilt yields fall as oil slides below $100
items.excerpt: UK 10-year gilt yields fell about eight basis points on Monday 21 September as oil resumed its slide, and extended the fall to 5.20%, their lowest since 8 September, early on Tuesday. Brent fell below $100 on reports that Iran could reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the US lifted its blockade of Iranian ports.

gb10y.mechanism: Cheaper oil lowers the UK inflation outlook, so investors accept a lower yield on gilts. A lower yield means gilt prices rose.
gb10y.outlook: The fall may not last: August borrowing came in at £18.3 billion, above the £15.5 billion expected, and Brent is rebounding. Next month’s Autumn Budget is the key test.

items.title: Canada 10Y bond yield hits 34-month high
items.excerpt: Canada’s 10-year government bond yield rose to 3.99%, the highest since November 2023, and has gained 36.3 basis points over the past four weeks. The Bank of Canada faces inflation concerns while energy prices remain elevated.

ca10y.mechanism: Canadian yields followed the US Treasury selloff, where the 10-year hit its highest since 2007 on strong data and a weak auction. Elevated energy prices also make a Bank of Canada hike more likely, which pushes yields up.
ca10y.outlook: Upward bias while US yields stay high and oil stays elevated. Easing oil prices, as happened after Iran-talk hopes, would pull the yield back from 4%.

items.title: Japan core CPI (Aug) 2.6%, up from 2.3%
items.excerpt: Japan’s August core CPI accelerated to 2.6% year on year from 2.3%. Newsquawk noted that such a sustained upward drift tends to bring forward speculation on the pace of Bank of Japan tightening, feeding first through JGB yields.

jp10y.mechanism: Faster inflation raises the expected path of Bank of Japan rates, already lifted to 1.25% on 18 September, so investors demand a higher JGB yield. US Treasury yields above 5% this week added to the upward pull.
jp10y.outlook: Upward bias while inflation keeps rising and US yields stay above 5%. The next Tokyo CPI and BOJ board comments are the checks.

items.title: Dogecoin jumped 14% with no Musk post behind it — $795M of liquidations did the work
items.excerpt: DOGE traded from an intraday low of $0.08536 to a high of $0.09784 as CoinGlass data showed about $795 million of crypto liquidations, roughly $667.7 million of them short positions. Bitcoin broke higher first, and DOGE futures open interest rose 15%, showing traders were adding leveraged exposure.

doge.mechanism: Traders who had bet on falling prices were forced to buy back when Bitcoin climbed past $85,000, and that forced buying lifted the most volatile coins most. Dogecoin, a high-beta meme coin, therefore rose far more than Bitcoin.
doge.outlook: Momentum can continue while leverage keeps building, but a rally driven by short squeezes fades when forced buying stops. Watch whether DOGE holds $0.10.

items.title: Dogecoin jumps to highest price in months
items.excerpt: Dogecoin spiked to an intraday high of $0.1059, its highest since June, after X announced trading partnerships with Gemini, Kraken, Coinbase, Moomoo and Interactive Brokers that let users trade from the timeline. Derivatives open interest jumped about 10% in a single hour to around $350 million.

doge.mechanism: X’s trading integrations brought new attention to the coin most linked to Musk, and leveraged buyers pushed it through the $0.10 level. Pepe and Shiba Inu also rose as the whole meme-coin group rallied.
doge.outlook: Leverage is doing much of the lifting, so the move can reverse quickly. The 50-day average is still below the 200-day, a longer-term bearish sign.

items.title: Crypto markets hammered as Avalanche and Dogecoin lead broad sell-off
items.excerpt: Losses spread across all eight major digital assets on Wednesday evening: Bitcoin fell 2.04% to $84,435.97, Ethereum 2.72% to $2,678.35, XRP 4.45% to $1.50 and Dogecoin 7.79% to $0.09. The report said the pattern, heavier losses in smaller tokens, pointed to market-wide de-risking rather than a coin-specific cause.

doge.mechanism: After two days of leveraged buying, the US bond selloff pushed investors out of risky assets, and long positions in DOGE were liquidated as it fell back below $0.10. The most speculative coins fell hardest.
doge.outlook: Further downside if Bitcoin keeps sliding. $0.095–$0.10 is the level traders are watching.

xrp.mechanism: The broad crypto sell-off on Wednesday evening in New York, 24 September in HKT, pulled XRP down with Bitcoin. Rising US yields made risky assets less attractive.
xrp.outlook: US spot-XRP ETF inflows continued ($14.89 million on 24 September), which may limit the decline.

eth.mechanism: The Treasury selloff that day, with the 10-year yield at its highest since 2007, pushed investors out of risky assets, and Ether fell with Bitcoin. The decline was broad rather than specific to Ethereum.
eth.outlook: Further weakness if yields keep rising. A stable Bitcoin above $84,000 would limit it.

items.title: XRP price rallies amid renewed institutional demand
items.excerpt: XRP rose about 4% to $1.57 as trading volume climbed 55.85% to about $7.37 billion. US spot XRP ETFs took in about $52.95 million this week, their 11th consecutive week of inflows, and wallets holding 1–10 million XRP accumulated 470 million tokens, worth over $724 million, in the five days to Thursday (Santiment).

xrp.mechanism: Steady ETF inflows and large holders buying reduce the XRP available to sell, so the price rises. The rally held even though Bitget, an exchange, was hacked for about $157 million of tokens.
xrp.outlook: Upward bias while ETF inflows continue. $1.60 is resistance; a failure there would leave XRP range-bound.

items.title: Dogecoin hits $0.10 after 15% rally: can DOGE hold the breakout?
items.excerpt: Dogecoin surged more than 15% to just above $0.10, outperforming every major cryptocurrency tracked by CoinDesk, as Bitcoin held above $85,600 and more than $1 billion in crypto positions were liquidated over 24 hours, including $844 million of bearish bets. X’s new trading partnerships added attention to the meme coin.

doge.mechanism: Most of the week’s gain came on Monday and Tuesday, when forced short covering and X’s trading integrations pushed DOGE through $0.10. Wednesday’s broad crypto sell-off took back part of it, and the rest held.
doge.outlook: Holding the weekly gain needs real spot buying once short covering fades. Whether $0.10 becomes support is the test.

items.title: Gold caps weekly loss as Fed bets, 5.2% yields limit rebound
items.excerpt: Spot gold was near $4,289.70 an ounce, up 0.38%, as oil fell on renewed US–Iran diplomacy hopes, while rising Treasury yields and Fed rate-hike expectations capped the rebound. Fed funds futures priced about a 68.6% chance of another hike next month, the 10-year yield reached the 5.2% area, its highest since 2007, and one-year inflation expectations rose to 4.6%.

au.mechanism: Cheaper oil eased some of the inflation fear behind the rate-hike bets, and a softer dollar made gold cheaper for non-US buyers, so bargain hunters returned. Gold pays no interest, so a 10-year yield near 5.2% kept the rebound small.
au.outlook: Range-bound while yields stay above 5%: the next Fed signal and the August PCE inflation report decide the direction. Support is near $4,298 on futures.

items.title: Silver bounces as yields, dollar and crude back off
items.excerpt: Spot silver bounced from the $63 area on Friday, where buyers had also stepped in after the 16 September Fed decision, as the dollar, Treasury yields and crude oil all backed off together. Thursday’s drop was not silver-specific: rising crude lifted the 10-year yield near 5.15% and the 30-year to 5.446%, and the whole metals complex gave ground.

ag.mechanism: Lower crude reduced the inflation worry driving yields higher, and a weaker dollar makes silver cheaper for foreign buyers. Silver swings more than gold, so it bounced harder once that pressure paused.
ag.outlook: Fragile: another oil rally could lift yields and send silver back toward $62.98. Holding above that level keeps the 50-day average in play.

items.title: COMEX copper stays pressured around the $6.7 mark
items.excerpt: COMEX copper futures were pressured by surging yields and a firm dollar, slipping from record highs to $6.77 a pound, down 0.29% on the day. US stocks had recovered from their lows on Thursday, with the Nasdaq and S&P 500 closing roughly flat.

cu.mechanism: Higher US yields point to slower growth and raise the cost of holding metal, and a firm dollar makes dollar-priced copper dearer for other buyers. Both pulled copper back from its record high.
cu.outlook: Pressure stays while yields rise and the dollar stays firm. A retreat in yields would let copper move back toward its record.

items.title: Bitcoin price near $84K as macro pressures weigh on sentiment
items.excerpt: Bitcoin dipped to $83,229 at about 10:05 a.m. EST before stabilising near $84,000, having given back most of Monday’s $5,000-plus surge after failing a second time above $87,000. Block Scholes said rising US bond yields and $100 oil created strong macroeconomic pressure, while spot ETF inflows earlier in the week were the largest since October.

btc.mechanism: Bond yields above 5% make a non-yielding asset like Bitcoin less attractive, and $100 oil keeps the Fed leaning toward more hikes. Profit-taking after the failed push above $87,000 added to the selling.
btc.outlook: Spot ETF inflows and Strategy’s first Bitcoin purchase in nearly a month support the price. A further rise in yields would test the $83,000 area again.

items.title: Crypto market: altcoins start rotation rally, DeFi tokens rally broadly
items.excerpt: According to HTX data, Bitcoin fell below $84,000 to $83,900 and Ethereum traded at $2,688, while SOL surged past $120 with a 24-hour gain of 3.4% and BNB traded at $776. Total crypto market value rose 0.3% to $2.989 trillion as money rotated into DeFi tokens such as ENA (+13.94%), JTO (+13.38%) and JUP.

sol.mechanism: Money rotating out of Bitcoin into DeFi tokens favours Solana, whose network hosts many of them, including JTO and JUP. That demand lifted SOL above $120.
sol.outlook: Upward bias while the altcoin rotation lasts. A renewed fall in Bitcoin would likely pull SOL back below $120.

eth.mechanism: Ether stayed near $2,690 because the new buying went into smaller DeFi tokens rather than the two largest coins. Bitcoin’s slip below $84,000 held it back.
eth.outlook: Flat-to-firm while DeFi activity grows. It follows Bitcoin if yields push risk assets lower again.

bnb.mechanism: BNB held near $776 while new buying went into smaller DeFi tokens rather than the largest coins.
bnb.outlook: Little changed unless the altcoin rotation broadens to larger coins, or Bitcoin falls further.

items.title: Crypto prices on September 26: BTC 0.51% lower, SEI 23.58% higher
items.excerpt: At 10:30 a.m. KST on 26 September (CoinMarketCap), Bitcoin fell 0.51% to $84,057.48 while Dogecoin rose 3.35% to $0.09921, XRP 2.49% to $1.57 and Solana 4.05% to $122.12. The report said buying interest concentrated on selected altcoins while Bitcoin corrected around $84,000.

doge.mechanism: Money rotating from Bitcoin into selected altcoins lifted Dogecoin back toward $0.10, recovering part of Wednesday’s sell-off.
doge.outlook: Whether DOGE can retake $0.10 is the test. A further Bitcoin slide would pull it back.

items.title: XRP surges 16% this week, reclaims $1.55 after $157 million theft
items.excerpt: Lookonchain tracked 102.93 million XRP, worth about $157 million and 44% of the funds stolen from Bitget’s hot and warm wallets, which are still sitting in a handful of hacker wallets. XRP had risen 16% over the week, from a $1.25 low on 16 September to $1.66 on 23 September, dipped to $1.45 when the hack broke on 24 September and recovered to $1.55.

xrp.mechanism: After a 16% weekly rise, traders face the risk that the hacker sells the stolen 102.93 million XRP on the market, so buyers hold back and the price slips.
xrp.outlook: XRP holds above $1.55 if the wallets holding the stolen coins stay inactive. If the attacker starts selling, 24/7 Wall St. sees a drop toward the $1.45 low of 24 September.

items.title: Dogecoin swings 8.72%: mean-reversion of a crowded trade
items.excerpt: DOGE slid from about $0.10–$0.104 to about $0.095 over 11 hours to 3:06 p.m. UTC on 23 September, after breaking above long-term resistance near $0.095 and touching about $0.1059. CoinMarketCap said the move was the unwinding of an X-driven, leverage-heavy breakout as traders took profits, with the altcoin market cap down about 1.7% and no fresh Dogecoin-specific negative news.

doge.mechanism: Buyers who had piled in with borrowed money above $0.10 sold as the price slipped back below that level, and their stop-losses and liquidations pushed it lower. The whole altcoin market was also cooling that day.
doge.outlook: The $0.095–$0.10 band decides the next move: holding it keeps the breakout alive, losing it opens a deeper pullback.

items.title: JGB yields jump as inflation worries resurface
items.excerpt: Japanese government bond yields jumped on Thursday 24 September, the first trading day after the Bank of Japan raised its policy rate to 1.25% from 1% and after markets were closed through Wednesday for public holidays. The 10-year JGB yield rose 10 basis points to 3.075%, its highest since August 1996, and the five-year yield rose 10 basis points to a record 2.375%, on renewed concerns about inflation.

jp10y.mechanism: Tokyo was shut Monday to Wednesday while US Treasury yields jumped, so JGBs priced in three days of global selling at once on reopening. A weaker yen raises import prices and the chance of further Bank of Japan hikes, so investors demanded a higher yield.
jp10y.outlook: Upward bias while inflation worries and US yields above 5% persist. Bank of Japan bond-buying operations and officials’ comments on the yield level are the checks.

items.title: Euro zone yields fall after Iran raises prospect of Hormuz reopening
items.excerpt: Euro zone bond yields fell for a second straight day on Tuesday 22 September, to their lowest in almost two weeks, after Iran raised the prospect of reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington hinted it could restart talks with Tehran, pushing oil lower. Germany’s 10-year yield fell 1 basis point to 3.44% after rising as much as 4 basis points earlier, following a 7-basis-point fall on Monday. Traders priced about 35 basis points of further ECB tightening this year, down from 40 on Friday.

de10y.mechanism: The euro area imports most of its energy, so cheaper oil lowers expected inflation. Traders then priced less ECB tightening (35 bp instead of 40 bp), and lower expected policy rates pulled 10-year yields down.
de10y.outlook: Yields stay tied to oil and Hormuz headlines: a failed reopening or an oil rebound would push them back up, as happened intraday on Tuesday.

items.title: US Treasury yields rise as 30-year yield hits 22-year high
items.excerpt: US Treasury yields turned mixed on Friday 25 September: the 20- and 30-year yields rose while shorter maturities eased. The 30-year yield peaked at 5.5016%, its highest since June 2004. Consumer sentiment weakened and one-year inflation expectations rose from 4% to 4.6% (five-year from 3.3% to 3.4%), while hawkish Fed speakers after last week’s 25 bp hike lifted year-end tightening odds.

us30y.mechanism: Higher household inflation expectations raise the compensation investors want for holding a 30-year bond, so the long end sold off even as short maturities eased. Hawkish Fed comments after the September hike added to the pressure.
us30y.outlook: Upward bias while inflation expectations climb and Fed officials lean toward another hike. Next week’s August PCE inflation data is the test.

items.title: Canada 10-year yield eases from 3-year high
items.excerpt: Canada’s 10-year government bond yield eased to around 3.92% on 25 September after touching a near three-year high of 4% on 24 September. Falling oil prices, on hopes that US–Iran talks could reopen the Strait of Hormuz, tempered inflation concerns and paused the global bond selloff.

ca10y.mechanism: Cheaper oil lowers the inflation outlook, so the extra yield investors had demanded during the week’s selloff was partly given back. The yield fell even though it is still well above early-September levels.
ca10y.outlook: The pullback holds if oil keeps falling and Hormuz talks progress. A rebound in oil, or a strong retail-sales print, would push the yield back toward 4%.

items.title: Natural gas drops as the pipeline returns and the October contract expires
items.excerpt: November natural gas futures were down 3.66% at $3.107 by 17:10 GMT on Monday after Columbia Gas Transmission found the leak behind last week's force majeure and expected repairs to be done by Monday. October futures expired the same day, and milder Midwest and East Coast forecasts cut early heating demand. Lower-48 output was 110.6 Bcf per day and the gas rig count rose to 135, a three-year high.

ng.mechanism: The West Virginia pipeline outage that lifted gas last week was fixed, and milder forecasts cut heating demand. The dashboard's 6.13% drop is the expiring October contract's last day, while November fell about 3.7%.
ng.outlook: Mild weather and near-record output leave buyers little to work with. The Thursday EIA storage report and any delay to the repair are the next tests.

points.text: October gas futures expired on Monday, so the front-month price still showed October, which settled at $3.00 for the 6.13% drop, while November, the next contract, fell a smaller 3.7% to about $3.11.

Columbia Gas Transmission found the leak that had put up to 1.8 Bcf per day (billion cubic feet a day) of West Virginia pipeline capacity at risk and expected repairs by Monday, so the extra price added during last week's outage disappeared.
Updated 6-to-10 and 8-to-14 day forecasts turned milder across the Midwest and East Coast, which took early October heating demand out of the outlook and pushed gas lower.
Output stayed near record at 110.6 Bcf per day and Baker Hughes counted 135 gas rigs, a three-year high, which gave sellers more confidence.
Traders who had bought before the outage used the October expiry to sell and take profits, which added to the drop.

nextPoints.text: Lean lower for the next few sessions, because mild weather and near-record output leave little extra demand for gas.
News that the pipeline repair is running late, or colder Midwest forecasts, would bring buyers back.
The EIA weekly storage report on Thursday 1 October, where analysts expected a 55 to 65 Bcf build.

items.title: Oil falls as Saudi pipeline restart lifts Middle East exports
items.excerpt: US West Texas Intermediate crude fell $3.22, or 3.5%, to $89.38 on Tuesday, and Brent settled $2.69 lower at $102.59. Saudi Arabia resumed tanker loadings at its Red Sea port of Yanbu after restarting the East-West Pipeline, and Kpler data showed Middle East crude exports recovered to 16.328 million barrels per day in September, the highest since the war began in late February.

wti.mechanism: More Gulf oil reached the market after Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West Pipeline, and ongoing US-Iran talks lowered the risk premium. WTI fell 3.5% to $89.38.
wti.outlook: Prices lean lower while Gulf exports keep recovering. A new tanker attack or a collapse in talks would reverse that.

points.text: Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West Pipeline and resumed tanker loadings at the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which eased fears of a shortage and pushed WTI down $3.22 to $89.38.
Kpler data showed Middle East crude exports recovered to 16.3 million barrels per day in September, the most since the war began in late February, so buyers felt less pressure to pay up.
Media reports said the US could consider sanctions relief for Iran in talks to end the war, which made traders price in less risk of more lost supply, even though Trump denied offering concessions.
Dennis Kissler of BOK Financial said bigger flows through the Saudi pipeline and the continuing US-Iran talks were the main reasons crude fell.

nextPoints.text: Lean lower while Gulf exports keep recovering, because more barrels are reaching buyers.
A new attack on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz or a breakdown in US-Iran talks would push prices back up.
The EIA weekly US inventory report on Wednesday 30 September, where a Reuters poll expected crude and gasoline stocks to fall.

items.title: Wheat falls on USDA report day even with tighter stocks

also.title: Corn Collapse on Wednesday, as USDA Reports Larger than Expected Stocks

items.excerpt: December CBOT wheat closed at $6.75¾, down 17 cents, as the wheat complex ignored a USDA Grain Stocks report showing September 1 wheat stocks of 1.846 billion bushels, 288 million below a year ago and under estimates. The NASS Small Grains Summary put all-wheat production at 1.534 billion bushels, up 3 million from August and slightly above trade estimates. KC and Minneapolis wheat also closed lower.

wh.mechanism: Wheat fell 17 cents to $6.75¾ on USDA report day even though wheat stocks came in tighter than expected. Corn fell hard on a big stocks surprise, and the whole grain group traded lower.
wh.outlook: Wheat falling on a supportive number points to a soft few sessions. Strong export sales would be the first sign of buyers returning.

points.text: USDA's quarterly Grain Stocks report put September 1 wheat stocks at 1.846 billion bushels, 288 million below a year ago and under estimates, but traders ignored this tighter number and December wheat still fell 17 cents to $6.75¾.
The same morning, the Small Grains Summary put 2026 wheat production at 1.534 billion bushels, slightly above trade estimates, which gave sellers a small supply argument.
Corn fell 21¼ cents the same day after USDA found 2.095 billion bushels of corn in storage, 184 million more than expected, and wheat fell with the rest of the grain group.
SovEcon cut its Russian wheat export forecast by 4.7 million tonnes to 36.7 million, which should help US sales later, but it did not stop Wednesday's drop.

nextPoints.text: Lean flat to lower in the next few sessions, because wheat fell even on a supportive stocks number.
Strong US export sales or more cuts to Russian exports would give buyers a reason to return.
The USDA Export Sales report on Thursday 1 October, with traders looking for 250,000 to 450,000 tonnes of wheat sales.

items.title: Oil jumps as a third US aircraft carrier heads to the Middle East
items.excerpt: West Texas Intermediate futures climbed 2.7% to settle at $92.87 a barrel on Thursday and Brent jumped 4.4% to $102.31 after US officials told the Wall Street Journal that the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group, Marine Corps ships and up to 10,000 more troops are heading to the Middle East. At least three tankers came under attack this week trying to pass the Strait of Hormuz.

wti.mechanism: A report that the US is sending a third carrier group and more troops raised the risk of a wider war with Iran. Tanker attacks near Hormuz and tight fuel supply added to the worry, lifting WTI 2.7% to $92.87.
wti.outlook: The military buildup keeps a war-risk premium in prices. Progress in US-Iran talks or a big emergency stock release would take it out.

points.text: US officials said the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier group and up to 10,000 more troops are heading to the Middle East, which raised fears of a wider war with Iran and lifted WTI 2.7% to $92.87.
At least three tankers were attacked this week while trying to pass the Strait of Hormuz, so traders worried that Gulf flows, which had just recovered to prewar levels, could break down again.
Russia's ban on diesel exports after Ukrainian strikes on its refineries kept US diesel near a record at $6.40 a gallon, which added to the supply worries behind crude.
Chinese refiners canceled some gasoline and jet fuel exports planned for October, which made the world fuel market look even tighter.

nextPoints.text: Lean higher while the US military buildup grows, because traders are pricing a bigger risk of new fighting with Iran.
A real step forward in US-Iran talks or a large release of government oil stocks would pull prices back.
The EIA weekly US petroleum inventory report on Wednesday 7 October.

items.title: Natural gas bounces back above $3 as sellers run out of room

also.title: Nat-Gas Prices Fall on Larger Weekly Storage Build and Seasonal US Weather

items.excerpt: Sellers pushed November natural gas under $3.00 on Friday to an intraday low of $2.912, just ahead of September's main bottoms, before buyers stepped in and the contract traded at $3.026, up 1.99%, at 18:09 GMT. FXEmpire called it a trade off the September lows, not a new weather story. Thursday's EIA report showed a 64 Bcf build, leaving storage 2.4% above the five-year average.

ng.mechanism: After Thursday's storage-driven drop, sellers pushed gas to $2.912, near September's lows, and then short sellers bought back. Hints of a cooler Midwest in mid-October made them less willing to stay short.
ng.outlook: Mild October weather, high output and a storage cushion still face buyers. The bounce needs colder forecasts to last.

points.text: Thursday's EIA report showed a 64 Bcf (billion cubic feet) build for the week to September 25, one more than expected, which pushed gas down 1.93% on Thursday and set up Friday's bounce from a lower level.
Sellers pushed November gas under $3.00 to $2.912, just above September's lows, and then short sellers (traders betting on a fall) bought back, which lifted the price 2.43% to about $3.04.
Some longer-range weather models showed a cooler Midwest for October 8 to 15, which could add heating demand, so short sellers did not want to stay exposed below $3.00.
The price added for last week's Columbia Gas pipeline outage was gone by Friday's low, so the bounce started from a level with no outage premium left in it.

nextPoints.text: Lean sideways to lower, because mild October weather, high output and a storage cushion still limit demand.
Colder Midwest forecasts that hold run after run would turn the bounce into a longer rally.
The EIA weekly storage report on Thursday 8 October.

items.title: Silver loses about 6% in a week of high US yields and a strong dollar

also.title: Silver prices today, Monday, September 28, 2026: Silver prices slump as oil prices and higher-rate expectations rise

items.excerpt: Spot silver fell 1.1% to $60.17 on Friday, and Reuters said silver, platinum and palladium were all set for weekly losses as a stronger dollar and elevated Treasury yields hit metals that pay no interest. The 10- and 30-year Treasury yields hit their highest levels since 2002 on Thursday. On Monday, Yahoo Finance reported silver futures sliding to $61.75 after Trump rejected another chance to end the Iran war, oil rose back above $100 and markets priced a 70.3% chance of an October Fed hike.

ag.mechanism: Silver fell about 6.2% for the week, with Monday's 4.71% drop doing most of it as oil above $100 raised bets on a Fed rate hike. High Treasury yields and a stronger dollar were the common thread on the down days.
ag.outlook: Rate-hike odds fell to 22% after a weak jobs report, but yields are still high. Silver is holding near $60 ahead of the late-October Fed meeting.

points.text: Monday did most of the damage, as silver fell 4.71% after oil rose back above $100 and markets priced a 70.3% chance of an October Fed rate hike, which makes a metal that pays no interest less attractive.
Silver lost another 0.90% on Tuesday and 0.94% on Wednesday as Treasury yields kept rising, with the 10- and 30-year yields reaching their highest levels since 2002 on Thursday.
The US dollar headed for a weekly gain, and a stronger dollar makes silver cost more for buyers using other currencies, which kept pressure on the price all week.
On Friday, US payrolls rose only 29,000 against 90,000 expected, which first lifted silver 2% to $62.07, but it then fell back to $60.17 as the dollar and yields stayed high.

nextPoints.text: Lean flat to lower near $60, because Treasury yields are still close to their highest since 2002 even after the weak jobs report.
If Fed hike odds keep falling from 22% and yields drop, silver could bounce from the $60 level.
The Federal Reserve's policy meeting on October 27–28.

items.title: Yen jumps after Japan's currency chief says take the US-Japan warning seriously

also.title: Europe Roundup: Sterling weakens against the dollar, Europe's stocks climbs, Gold ticks up, Oil falls - September 29th, 2026
Week Ahead: Fed Minutes in the Spotlight

items.excerpt: The yen rose against all major currencies on Monday and pushed USD/JPY through 157 after Vice Finance Minister Atsushi Mimura said markets should take the "very clear message" from Japan and the US on yen weakness "at face value". He said he had "absolutely no such concern" about Japan's capacity to intervene again. At the same time Brent rose 2.49% to $106.92 and the US 10-year Treasury yield stayed above 5.2%.

jpy.mechanism: Japan's top currency official warned that Tokyo and Washington were serious about stopping the yen's fall, so traders bought yen out of fear of intervention and USD/JPY fell 0.85%. High US yields stopped the yen from gaining more.
jpy.outlook: The intervention threat should keep USD/JPY capped, but a lasting yen rally needs the US-Japan interest-rate gap to shrink.

points.text: Currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura told markets to take the joint Japan-US warning on the weak yen "at face value", so traders bought yen in case Tokyo stepped in and USD/JPY fell 0.85% to below 157.

Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama and US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had said in talks on Friday that the yen was undervalued, so Monday's warning carried more weight because Washington was on Tokyo's side.

The Bank of Japan's hike to 1.25% earlier in September had not stopped the yen's slide because US rates stay much higher, so Monday's drop in USD/JPY came from the intervention threat and not from a smaller rate gap.
On the US side, the 10-year Treasury yield stayed above 5.2% and the 2-year near 4.9% as Brent oil rose to $106.92, which kept demand for dollars strong and limited how far USD/JPY could fall.

nextPoints.text: USD/JPY is likely to stay capped below 158 while officials keep warning, but high US yields make a big yen rally unlikely without real intervention.
If US yields keep rising on oil and Fed hike bets and Tokyo only talks, traders could test the warning and push USD/JPY back up.
Wednesday 7 October: Japan publishes August wage growth and the Fed releases the minutes of its September meeting.

items.title: Franc slips to a four-month low as US yields rise and the SNB stays at zero

also.title: Dollar set for big rise in September, mainly at euro's expense
Kinzey Capital Management Eyes SNB Hold and Inflation Forecast

items.excerpt: The dollar rose on Tuesday as volatile oil prices and a rapid climb in Treasury yields lent support, and the Swiss franc weakened to 0.8335 per dollar, its softest in four months. The US two-year yield was at its highest in two years and close to 5%. Markets saw a more than 70% chance of a Fed hike at the end of October, up from 57% a week earlier, according to CME FedWatch.

chf.mechanism: US yields rose on Fed hike bets while the Swiss National Bank keeps its rate at 0%, so the gap between the two made dollars more attractive than francs and USD/CHF rose 0.24%.
chf.outlook: USD/CHF leans higher while the rate gap stays this wide, but softer US data or a rush into safe assets could pull it back.

points.text: The US two-year Treasury yield rose to a two-year high near 5% and markets put the chance of an October Fed hike above 70%, so holding dollars paid more and USD/CHF rose 0.24%.

The Swiss National Bank kept its rate at 0% on 24 September, while the ECB sits at 2.5% and the Fed at 3.75% to 4.00%, so francs earn almost nothing and investors sold them for higher-paying currencies.

With Japan threatening to defend the yen, traders have started borrowing in francs instead of yen to fund carry trades (borrowing a low-rate currency to buy a higher-rate one), which adds steady selling of the franc.
The dollar also rose against the euro and the pound on Tuesday as Brent stayed above $106 a barrel, so the franc's fall was part of a broad dollar gain and not a Swiss-only story.

nextPoints.text: USD/CHF leans higher while US rates stay far above the SNB's 0%.
Weak US data that cuts Fed hike bets, or investors buying francs as a safe place during a bond selloff, would push USD/CHF back down.

items.title: Aussie is the weakest major as soft core inflation backs a cautious RBA

also.title: Asia Roundup: Australian dollar dips after Australian inflation data, Asia stocks gain, Gold firm, Oil gains - September 30th, 2026
RBA Hiked Unanimously, Then Bullock's 'Hope' Sent Aussie Through 0.7000 Support

items.excerpt: Australia's headline CPI rose to 4.0% y/y in August as expected, but the trimmed mean rose only 0.2% on the month against a 0.3% forecast. The Aussie was the weakest major currency even though softer US PCE inflation (core 0.2% m/m vs 0.3% expected) cut October Fed hike odds from about 51% to 37.1% and weakened the dollar.

aud.mechanism: Soft core inflation backed RBA Governor Bullock's hint that Tuesday's hike may be the last, so traders cut bets on another rise and sold the Aussie, which fell 0.39% even as the US dollar weakened.
aud.outlook: AUD/USD leans lower while markets doubt a November RBA hike, unless new data revives those bets.

points.text: The RBA raised its cash rate to 4.60% on Tuesday, but Governor Michele Bullock said the "hope" is that this will be "restrictive enough", so traders cut bets on more hikes and kept selling AUD/USD on Wednesday.

August trimmed-mean inflation (a core measure that drops the biggest price swings) rose only 0.2% against a 0.3% forecast, which cut the market's chance of a November RBA hike to 20% from 36% and pulled AUD/USD down 0.39%.
Headline inflation jumped to 4.0% mostly because car fuel prices rose 14.8% in August, and traders treated that as an energy effect and not a reason for more RBA hikes, so it gave the Aussie no lift.
Softer US PCE inflation cut October Fed hike odds from about 51% to 37.1% and weakened the dollar, yet AUD/USD still fell because the repricing of the RBA was the bigger force.

nextPoints.text: AUD/USD leans lower while markets doubt the RBA will hike again in November.
Hotter Australian inflation data or RBA speeches that bring November hike bets back would support the Aussie.

items.title: Aussie drops as a small trade surplus meets a global bond selloff

also.title: America's Roundup: Dollar hits 17-month high versus euro, US stocks inch up, Gold edges higher, Oil jumps 4%
Bond Rout Extends Into Q4 as Dollar Rises and EUR/USD Breaks 1.13

items.excerpt: Australia's goods trade surplus shrank to A$495 million in August from a revised A$1.4 billion in July, well below the A$2.0 billion forecast, as imports jumped 5.8%, led by a 79% rise in computer equipment for data centres. Later on Thursday a global bond selloff pushed the US 10-year Treasury yield to about 5.34%, a 24-year high, and the dollar extended its broad gains.

aud.mechanism: A weak Australian trade number and a soft factory survey hit the Aussie, then a global bond selloff lifted US yields to their highest since 2002 and pulled money into the dollar, so AUD/USD fell 0.62%.
aud.outlook: AUD/USD leans lower while US long-term yields and oil stay high, and Friday's US jobs report is the next test.

points.text: A global bond selloff pushed the US 10-year Treasury yield to about 5.34%, its highest since 2002, which drew money into the dollar and pushed AUD/USD down 0.62%.
The Aussie actually rose a little in Asian trading even after weak local data, and the 0.62% fall came later in London and New York hours as US yields climbed.

Australia's manufacturing PMI (a monthly survey of factory managers) fell to 49.6, below the 50 line between growth and shrinking, which added to the soft local data behind the Aussie's slide this week.

The US ISM survey's prices-paid index jumped to 77.9 from 71.1 and Brent moved back above $100 after Chinese refiners suspended fuel exports, which kept US inflation fears and yields high and helped the dollar against the Aussie.

nextPoints.text: AUD/USD leans lower while the US 10-year yield stays above 5.3% and oil stays near $100.
A weak US jobs report that pulls Treasury yields down would give the Aussie room to bounce.
Friday 2 October: the US September jobs report (nonfarm payrolls).

items.title: Aussie bounces as a weak US jobs report knocks the dollar

also.title: Bond Rout Extends Into Q4 as Dollar Rises and EUR/USD Breaks 1.13
Week Ahead: Fed Minutes in the Spotlight

items.excerpt: US payrolls rose just 29,000 in September against a 90,000 consensus, unemployment edged up to 4.2%, wages undershot and earlier months were revised lower. Treasury yields fell, expectations for an October Fed hike collapsed into the low teens, US equity futures rallied and the Dollar Index fell back below 102. Over the weekend President Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, so US crude futures jumped more than 4% early on Monday and investors sold bonds to guard against higher inflation.
Government bond yields in other countries also rose on Monday as worries about government debt and sticky inflation hit bonds worldwide, which added to selling in Treasuries.
The 10-year yield gave back part of its rise from 5.27% after an official said Qatari mediators would hold new talks with Iran and the US, which pulled oil back to almost flat.

nextPoints.text: The 10-year yield is likely to stay near 5.2% to 5.3% in the next few sessions because traders still expect a Fed hike by December even after Friday's weak jobs report.
A US-Iran deal that reopens the Strait of Hormuz would pull oil lower and remove the main source of inflation fear, which would bring yields down.
Wednesday 7 October: the Fed publishes the minutes of its September meeting, which will show how many officials want more hikes.

items.title: Canada's 10-year yield climbs toward 4% as US bond selling resumes

also.title: 30-year Treasury bond yield scales to highest level since 2002

items.excerpt: Canada's 10-year government bond yield rose to near 4% in late September, approaching a three-year high, as the US Treasury selloff resumed. Advance estimates showed real GDP rose 0.2% in August after an unchanged July, in line with expectations and pointing to a Bank of Canada hold.

ca10y.mechanism: Selling in US Treasuries resumed on Tuesday and Canadian bonds were pulled along. The 10-year yield rose about 3 basis points to near 4%, close to a three-year high.
ca10y.outlook: Canadian yields are likely to keep following US Treasuries because local data have matched forecasts. A sharp fall in oil would ease the inflation fears behind the selling.

points.text: Selling of US Treasuries resumed on Tuesday, with the US 30-year yield touching 5.6% for the first time since 2002, and Canadian bonds followed, lifting the 10-year yield about 3 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to near 4%.
Oil price gains tied to the Middle East war kept investors expecting central banks, including the Fed, to raise rates further, which kept pressure on government bonds such as Canada's.

Statistics Canada's GDP figures (flat in July, up an estimated 0.2% in August) matched forecasts and pointed to a Bank of Canada hold, so the rise in the yield came from abroad rather than from local data.

nextPoints.text: Canadian yields are likely to keep tracking US Treasuries in the next few sessions because local data have been in line with forecasts.
A sharp fall in oil prices would ease inflation fears and pull Canadian yields down along with US yields.
Wednesday 28 October: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement and Monetary Policy Report.

items.title: JGB yields fall after report that PM Takaichi will promise a quick response to market swings

also.title: Global market: Japan 10-year bond yield heads for record fifth quarterly gain

items.excerpt: Japanese government bond yields extended declines on Wednesday after the Nikkei reported that Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi will pledge a nimble response to unexpected market moves in an October 5 policy speech. The 10-year JGB yield slipped 3.5 basis points to 3.05%, and a modestly firm two-year bond auction also supported prices.

jp10y.mechanism: A report that PM Takaichi will promise to respond quickly to market swings and watch interest rates when setting debt issuance eased fears about Japan's finances. Lower odds of a Bank of Japan hike and a firm auction also helped, so the 10-year yield fell about 2 basis points to about 3.05%.
jp10y.outlook: JGB yields may hold near 3% while investors wait for Takaichi's 5 October speech. New spending without clear funding would push them back up.

points.text: New York Fed President John Williams cooled bets on an October Fed hike, and swaps cut the chance of a Bank of Japan hike in October to 23% from 36%, which pulled JGB yields lower.

The Nikkei reported that PM Takaichi will promise to respond swiftly to market swings and to size debt issuance with an eye on interest rates, which eased fears about Japan's finances and helped the 10-year yield fall about 2 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to about 3.05%.
A modestly firm two-year JGB auction showed solid demand for new government debt, which also supported bond prices and lowered yields.

nextPoints.text: The 10-year JGB yield may hold near 3% in the next few sessions as investors wait to hear what Takaichi actually promises.
If the speech brings new spending plans without clear funding, investors could sell JGBs again and push the 10-year yield back toward its highest levels since 1996.
Monday 5 October: Takaichi's policy speech on the first day of the extraordinary session of parliament.

items.title: Canadian bond yields fall sharply as US yields ease and factory growth slows

also.title: Canada Manufacturing Growth Falls to 6-Month Low
Treasury yields fall from multiyear highs

items.excerpt: Canadian government bond yields fell sharply on Thursday, with the two-year yield down 11 basis points to 3.264% and the 10-year down 6.1 basis points to 3.938% by early afternoon. The two-year led the decline as investors moved into shorter-dated government debt, after a volatile September in which the 10-year climbed to just above 4%.

ca10y.mechanism: US Treasury yields turned lower after hitting a 24-year high, and a weak Canadian factory survey pointed to slower growth. Buyers returned to Canadian bonds and the 10-year yield fell about 5 basis points.
ca10y.outlook: Canadian yields are likely to stay just below 4% because softer factory data argue against fast Bank of Canada hikes. Another jump in US yields or oil would push them back up.

points.text: The US 10-year Treasury yield touched its highest level since April 2002 on Thursday and then eased 5 basis points, and Canadian yields followed, with the 10-year down about 5 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) on the day.

The S&P Global Canada manufacturing index fell to 51.5 in September from 53.0, a six-month low, with export orders down for a fourth month, which pointed to slower growth and drew buyers to Canadian bonds.

The two-year yield, which tracks expectations for Bank of Canada rates, fell 11 basis points, about twice as much as the 10-year, so the strongest buying was in bonds most tied to the central bank's next moves.

nextPoints.text: The 10-year yield is likely to stay just below 4% in the next few sessions because weaker factory data argue against fast Bank of Canada hikes.
A fresh jump in oil prices or another surge in US Treasury yields would push the Canadian 10-year back above 4%.
Wednesday 28 October: Bank of Canada interest rate announcement and Monetary Policy Report.

items.title: Investors run to German bonds and euro-area yields drop despite higher inflation

also.title: Euro zone inflation surges, keeping pressure on ECB to hike

items.excerpt: Traders favoured safe-haven German debt over weaker countries such as France on Friday, and the German 10-year yield fell roughly 10 basis points to 3.4178%. Euro zone inflation jumped to 3.8% in September from 3.2%, above the 3.6% forecast, but core inflation rose only to 2.5%, and money markets pared bets on further ECB hikes.

de10y.mechanism: Traders cut bets on more ECB hikes and moved money out of French bonds into safe German ones. The German 10-year yield fell about 10 basis points and the euro-area AAA 10-year yield fell about 8 basis points to about 3.52%.
de10y.outlook: Euro-area AAA yields may stay below last week's highs while traders expect the ECB to wait. A further rise in energy prices could bring back bets on an October hike.

points.text: Money markets cut bets on more ECB rate hikes on Thursday and Friday, and a further hike is no longer fully priced until early 2027, which pulled euro-area yields down.

Headline inflation jumped to 3.8% in September on fuel and gas costs, but core inflation (which leaves out food and energy) rose only to 2.5% from 2.4%, so analysts called the underlying trend steady and bond buyers were not scared off.

Investors moved money from French bonds into German ones, which cut the German 10-year yield by about 10 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 3.42% and the euro-area AAA 10-year yield by about 8 basis points to about 3.52%.

France's 2027 budget bill, presented on Thursday with unpopular spending cuts, gave markets little relief, and the French-German 10-year gap rose above 150 basis points for the first time since late 2011 as more money went into German debt.

nextPoints.text: Euro-area AAA yields may stay below last week's highs in the next few sessions because traders now expect the ECB to wait until December or later before hiking again.
A further rise in energy prices in the next few weeks could make an October ECB hike likely again, as Capital Economics warned, and push yields back up.
Thursday 29 October: ECB interest rate decision at the end of its 28 to 29 October meeting in Frankfurt.

items.excerpt: Germany's 10-year yield, the euro zone benchmark, climbed to 3.65% on Monday, its highest since 2009, then fell as central bankers pushed back on fast rate hikes. On Friday traders favoured safe-haven German debt over French bonds and the German 10-year yield fell roughly 10 basis points to 3.4178%.

de10y.mechanism: The euro-area AAA 10-year yield fell about 10 basis points over the week, mostly on Friday with smaller falls on Tuesday and Wednesday. The common thread was traders scaling back bets on fast ECB hikes, and on Friday investors also moved money from French bonds into German ones.
de10y.outlook: Yields may stay below Monday's highs while traders expect the ECB to wait until December or later. Higher energy prices are the main risk to that view.

points.text: ECB President Christine Lagarde said on Monday a measured response was appropriate and policymaker Peter Kazimir said the ECB had time to be flexible, so traders cut hike bets and the yield fell on Tuesday, Wednesday and Friday.

New York Fed President John Williams said on Tuesday the Fed had time before hiking again, and energy prices fell that day, which helped the German 10-year yield drop 4 basis points (hundredths of a percentage point) to 3.57% on Wednesday.

On Thursday and Friday investors sold French bonds and bought German ones, pushing the French-German gap to its widest since late 2011, and Friday's flight to safety gave the week's biggest fall of about 8 basis points in the euro-area AAA yield.
September euro-zone inflation of 3.8% came in above the 3.6% forecast, but steady core inflation of 2.5% did not stop Friday's bond buying.

nextPoints.text: Euro-area AAA yields may stay below Monday's 2009-high levels in the next few sessions because traders no longer fully price another ECB hike until early 2027.
A new jump in oil and gas prices would revive inflation fears and bets on an October ECB hike, which would push yields back up.
Thursday 29 October: ECB interest rate decision at the end of its 28 to 29 October meeting in Frankfurt.

items.excerpt: The Nikkei 225 closed at 69,947 on Monday, up 1,637 points, after briefly recovering 70,000 for the first time in about three months. Weak US jobs data cut expectations for an October Fed rate hike, and Tokyo Electron, Advantest, SoftBank Group and TDK led the rise. The broader TOPIX rose 54.22 points to 4,145.22.

nky.mechanism: Friday's weak US jobs report cut bets on an October Fed hike, so money became easier to put into growth shares, and US tech gains carried into Tokyo's AI and chip names, which pushed the Nikkei up 2.40%.
nky.outlook: The Nikkei sits just under 70,000, so the Fed minutes on Wednesday and US chip stocks decide whether it closes above that level.

points.text: Friday's weak US September jobs report led investors to scale back bets on another Fed rate hike in October, so money became cheaper to borrow and easier to put into growth shares, which sent buying into Tokyo's AI and chip names and pushed the Nikkei up 2.40%.
US tech shares rose after the jobs data, so Tokyo followed that overnight move on Monday, which pushed the Nikkei briefly past 70,000 for the first time in about three months.
Advantest rose 4.32% and Tokyo Electron 5.5%, and because the Nikkei is price-weighted (higher-priced shares count for more), Advantest alone added about 360 points, which pushed the index up 2.40%.
The broader TOPIX rose a smaller 1.33%, so a few high-priced chip shares, not the whole market, did most of the work, which is how the Nikkei rose 2.40%.

The yen stayed weak at about 157.66 per dollar near the close, which usually helps exporters, but Japan.co.jp said the rally came from chip shares rather than a new fall in the yen, so the currency was not the extra push that lifted the Nikkei.

nextPoints.text: The Nikkei can hold near 70,000 while US chip stocks stay firm, because lower Fed-hike odds make AI shares easier to own.
Fed minutes that point to more rate hikes, or a new jump in oil from the Middle East, would bring back the rate fears that hit Tokyo in late September.
The minutes of the Fed's September meeting come out on Wednesday 7 Oct at 2 p.m. New York time, which is early Thursday morning in Tokyo.

items.excerpt: The Nikkei rose 737.12 points, or 1.05%, to close at 70,683.98 on Tuesday, a three-month high, after gains on Wall Street and a pullback in oil prices. The advance was wider than in recent sessions, with real estate, banking and textile stocks among the leaders. Taiyo Yuden was the top Nikkei gainer at midday, up 6.15% at 11,135 yen.

nky.mechanism: A record Nasdaq close and lower oil carried Monday's rally into Tuesday, so buying spread from the top chip names to electronics parts makers and banks, which pushed the Nikkei up 1.05% to close above 70,000.
nky.outlook: After a 2,374-point gain in two days, the Nikkei needs the Fed minutes and Japanese bond yields to stay calm to hold 70,000.

points.text: The Nasdaq hit a record high on Monday as SpaceX, Tesla, Nvidia and Broadcom rose, so Tokyo's AI and electronics shares followed that overnight move, which pushed the Nikkei up 1.05% on Tuesday.
Oil prices fell, and Japan imports nearly all of its oil, so cheaper crude lowered costs for Japanese companies, which helped push the Nikkei higher.

Buying spread beyond the biggest names, with Taiyo Yuden up 6.15% at midday and Advantest up 3.85% at the close, so the rally was wider than Monday's chip-led jump, which pushed the Nikkei up 1.05% even as SoftBank Group fell more than 3%.

The 10-year Japanese government bond yield closed near 3.09% after a new 10-year auction sold at an average 3.101%, so banks earn more on the loans they make, which helped bank shares join the rally and added to the Nikkei's 1.05% gain.
The yen weakened back above 158 per dollar in the Tokyo afternoon, so exporters' overseas earnings are worth more in yen, which added another lift to the Nikkei.

nextPoints.text: Expect a pause near 70,000, because the index gained 2,374 points in two days and chip leaders are ripe for profit-taking.
BOJ Governor Kazuo Ueda said on Tuesday the bank will keep raising rates, so a further jump in Japanese bond yields or a stronger yen could pull Tokyo back.
The Fed's September minutes come out on Wednesday 7 Oct, and Tokyo is closed on Monday 12 Oct for Sports Day.
